name: Jade Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play a junior viola part in a town chamber group, record slow practice parts and help the lead violist with two beginners. I finished secondary school and came to paid music after years in a shop; at 58 I still ask the lead to mark difficult bowings for me. I like seeing a new player hear the harmony under a tune.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps that schedule workable at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner drives a local bus on regular shifts and our children are grown. We rent a flat and have four months of expenses saved. Music pays about what this junior job usually does, with some similar groups nearby, but I still need a real booked place to earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chamber group that a quicker booking list is fine if the paid rehearsal is written beside it. An email does not hold a bow for a beginner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our four months saved and my partner’s regular driving wage make a delayed rehearsal fee manageable. I do not know yet what retirement will pay, so I still need the dates that are booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid group rehearsals, two beginner sessions under the lead and simple practice recordings this season. I use AI now and then for a calendar draft, then check the dates against the leader’s paper sheet; before next season I would ask for a written cancellation fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this mild change while the booked rehearsals pay. One late fee will not force us to borrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a rehearsal was cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall lost heat last winter and our fee was delayed. A written half-fee term would make the next cancellation easier to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the lead player check for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She marks the bow change I miss in a fast passage. A beginner can hear a wrong bow before I can explain it.

think: Our **four-month reserve** and partner wage cover one late fee.
I still need **paid dates** until actual retirement income is known.

Request a **written half-fee term** before next season.
feel: I feel **calm** while current rehearsals and household income hold.

fieldNote: Her **late junior role** pays a typical musician fee while she learns difficult bowings from the lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chamber manager that generated practice parts could replace small recorded jobs. I would ask for a written fee whenever the group books my playing or a beginner session.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The slow viola tracks bring about a quarter of my own pay. Four months saved could carry a search, but losing regular orders would make the rent account smaller each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask for three months of paid group calls and a paid demonstration of a new AI part checker from the lead violist, who has used it safely. In the first year I would test only my own nameless viola part under the group licence and approved local storage, play every changed bar against paper and stop if the range is wrong or the file leaves the group’s system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about those recording orders. I can learn a proven tool. An AI-checked viola part still needs a buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you upload a beginner’s playing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep the learners’ audio out of my test. The lead can show me enough with a clean part I own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the checker yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the group needs to cover the licence and teaching hour. If it asks me to buy a trial, I will use the paper part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the group that thinking AGI by 2028 could make slow viola parts cheaply. Robots able to play a viola follow around 2031, three years later, so the recording work could go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect practice-track orders to end in 2028, costing a quarter of my own pay. Paid chamber dates might also fall, but I will not count a nearby post as open until I see it advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would total recording invoices and request a signed paid group calendar. In the first year after 2028, if paid chamber calls fall too, I would seek a posted music-centre desk job only if my secondary schooling and shop experience meet its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus route works; I would keep group calls and assisted pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the expected recording loss, with four months saved and some nearby employers giving a search window. I would be alarmed if the live calls collapsed too, but that is not my forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop at 60 instead of applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read an actual pension statement before changing work. Four months saved is useful, but it will not pay years of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a desk course first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the posted job requirements. I will not buy a course for a vacancy that may accept my shop experience.

I would warn **recording work** could vanish before playing robots arrive.
think: I expect **practice tracks** to end in 2028, removing a quarter of my own music pay.
Paid **chamber cuts** remain possible, not certain, while current group calls stay booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the lead player that five years until AGI by 2031 lets us test a paid first-steps viola class. Playing robots follow around 2034, after practice software changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recorded lines could end in 2031. I can help new players hold and tune a viola, but the lead must teach anything past those first steps and be paid for her time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I would get written hire terms for a separate community hall before collecting six adult fees. I would offer a four-week viola first-steps class only if those fees cover room hire, a paid lead’s teaching and my setup and beginner work, with inspected loan violas or sound instruments adults own. In the first year after 2031, I would repeat only while six paid safe places still cover both musicians and room under written hall terms; I would keep regular paid group calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until both musicians are paid from real deposits. Five years until AGI lets me test a paid viola first-steps class without spending our rent reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the loan instruments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall technician must inspect strings, bridges and bows before anyone plays. If a loan fails, the adult needs a sound replacement viola or a paying replacement participant; below six paid safe places, I would defer and refund everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only four adults pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four fees cannot cover the room and paid lead player. I would refund all four and keep my assisted beginner sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to learn what retirement actually pays. Viola-playing robots follow around 2039, but a birthday does not settle rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need chamber and beginner pay. Four months saved and a partner wage help now, but I have not seen a pension statement that lets me name a stopping date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request my actual pension statement and save twenty percent of each extra paid wedding performance after rent, food and instrument repairs toward six months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid group calls while booked and offer a separate viola first-steps class only after written hall terms, if six adults prepay room, a paid experienced lead, my beginner setup and teaching, and safe inspected loan or sound own instruments. I would not stop paid work just because I turn 68. If fewer than six can pay after instrument checks, I would refund everyone and continue paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about distant work with current paid calls and four months saved. I would decide how much to slow down only after seeing actual pension and class fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra wedding pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then nothing from that source goes into savings. I would not move rent money into savings just to say I reached six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach advanced players by yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a paid experienced lead would take advanced teaching. I would keep my part at the first steps I can show well.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because practice-track pay could end before another paid role is posted. Signed chamber calls, an actual pension statement and a qualifying desk vacancy with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a musician can still be an apprentice at 58. I practise the slow bow every morning, and a paid rehearsal still matters more than a grand title.

headlineQuote: I practise the slow bow every morning, and a paid rehearsal still matters more than a grand title.
portrait: At **58**, Jade is a junior violist with secondary schooling, a partner, grown children and four months saved.
Her **typical musician pay** comes from chamber calls, simple tracks and assisted beginner sessions, with some nearby groups.
She uses **AI occasionally** for dates and trials a new checker only after paid lead instruction on owned nameless music.
She offers a **paid first-steps class** only with six prepayments, an experienced paid lead and safe instruments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end practice-track income before a posted paid desk role appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed chamber calls**, a real pension statement and a posted eligible desk job with written net replacement pay would help Jade.
